The NWS storm survey team observed widespread damage from Faithorn to Hermansville with several structures severely damaged and thousands of trees uprooted or snapped off.  Downed trees and powerlines resulted in impassable roads. |The NWS survey team also concluded that the damage was characteristic of intense straight line winds of 100 to 110 mph.  This is supported by radar data which showed a classic descending rear inflow jet (strong high altitude winds descending to the ground) surging northeastward across this area. In addition, the downed trees fell in mainly the same direction along with signs of divergent flow in the damage pattern.

Over 30 firefighters from the Michigan DNR and the Seney National Wildlife Refuge  fought and ultimately contained the 203-acre Creighton Swamp Wildfire over a four-day period which burned in a swamp north of Highway M-28 in northern Schoolcraft County. The fire burned in a remote area which was difficult to access, east of County Road 454.  No wheeled vehicles could access the fire so drones with infrared cameras were utilized to help delineate the full extent of the fire. DNR wetland bully engines from Gwinn and Newberry and a tractor plow from Shingleton were also utilized fighting the fire.  A lightning strike most likely caused the fire.

A 46-acre wildfire burned over a three-day period approximately three-quarters of a mile south of the 12 Mile Beach Campground or just south of the Pictured Rocks National Lakeshore in Alger County. The Michigan DNR, Burt Township Fire Department and the National Park Service crews responded to the fire and worked throughout the night to get the fire successfully contained and to ensure the safety of campers and park visitors. DNR crews manned a tractor plow and nine engines while fighting the fire. A cause of the wildfire was not immediately determined.

Storm total snowfall reports included 12-14 inches of wet snow in the Ironwood area and over 12 inches in Wakefield.  The heavy wet snow combined with north winds gusting near 30 mph caused power outages to more than 1000 customers during the event and  closed or delayed many Gogebic County schools on the 17th.

Storm total snowfall reports included nearly 14 inches of wet snow at Bergland Dam and 8 inches at Paulding.  The heavy wet snow combined with north winds gusting near 30 mph caused power outages to over 600 customers during the event and closed or delayed many schools on the 17th.

Two-day storm total snowfall reports included 14 inches of wet snow at Herman and Three Lakes and 12-16 inches in the Watton area.  The heavy wet snow combined with north winds gusting near 35 mph caused power outages and tree damage to hundreds of customers during the event.   North winds gusting near 35 mph caused power outages to hundreds of customers during the event and closed schools throughout the county on the 17th.

An estimated storm-total snowfall of 10 to 12 inches of wet heavy snow over much of southern Houghton County.  The heavy wet snow combined with north winds gusting near 30 mph caused power outages to hundreds of customers during the event, and closed schools on the 17th.
Wet snow amounts generally ranged from one to three inches during the event with the  greatest total of 3.8 inches measured at Painesdale.  North winds gusted to near 40 mph at times.

The Copper Harbor ASOS measured north wind gusts in excess of 45 mph throughout much of the period with a peak gust of 56 mph around 2 am on the 18th. Some minor tree damage occurred with the higher winds.

Wet snowfall totals over northern Iron County were estimated to be 4 to 7 inches during the event with locally higher amounts near 10 inches.  The wet snow combined with north winds gusting near 40 mph at times caused some tree damage and knocked power out to nearly 600 customers. One to locally four inch snow amounts were common over the southern part of the county.

Wet snowfall totals over northern Dickinson County were estimated to be 3 to 6 inches during the event with locally higher amounts near 8 inches. The wet snow combined with north winds gusting to 40 to 45 mph at times caused some tree damage and sporadic  power outages.

Two-day storm total accumulation of wet snowfall around Marquette County included between 13 and 18 inches near National Mine,  14 inches at Clarkburg,  13 inches at the National Weather Service in Negaunee Township and around 10 inches from Sands Township to near Little Lake. The Gogebic County Road Commission reported numerous secondary roads and a few county roads impassable from the 13th into the 17th.  Highway M-28 east of Sunday Lake in Wakefield was closed from the 16th into the 21st due to high water. Estimated countywide damages to highway infrastructure were in the millions of dollars.  Governor Whitmer declared a state of emergency in Gogebic County on April 14th due to severe and widespread flooding.

Michigan DOT closed Highway M-28 at Ewen due to snowmelt flooding over the bridge along the South Branch of the Ontonagon River from the 13th until the 18th.  Traffic was detoured via US-2 and US-45. Ontonagon County was added to the state emergency declaration by Governor Whitmer on the 21st to assist in flood recovery efforts.

Michigan DOT reported snowmelt flood water over US Highway 41 between 27.75 and US Highway 2 near Rapid River on the 13th.  Flooding was also reported along the Sturgeon River near Nahma Junction from the 15th through the 23rd.

Fairly widespread flooding was observed across a large portion of Marquette County with flooding observed along the Chocolay, Escanaba and Michigamme Rivers. Some of the most severe and longest-duration flooding was along the Michigamme River near Republic and Witch Lake.  On April 24th Marquette County officials described extensive and significant flooding damage to 25+ roads and 7+ crossings with damage estimates exceeding $7 million. Marquette County was added to the state of emergency declaration on 4/21 by Governor Whitmer to aid in flood recovery efforts.

A flash flood impacted the Lake Linden, MI area early on April 12th after a culvert under railroad tracks failed and released a flood wave resulting in an estimated $150,000 in|damages. The flooding prompted a state of emergency declaration for Houghton County by Governor Whitmer. The culvert was recently installed as part of repairs following the Father���s Day flooding in 2018.  There was also prolonged snowmelt flooding along the Sturgeon River which lasted through the 24th.
Flooding impacts were reported along the Sturgeon River from the 13th into the 24th.

County Road 577 in Vulcan was also closed from the 15th into the 17th due to high water.  Governor Whitmer declared a state of emergency for Dickinson County on the 21st to open up state funds to assist in flood recovery efforts.
A few secondary roads were closed north of Newberry due to snowmelt runoff over the roads.

While MDOT was already planning on a $2.9 million project to remove and replace the bridge this summer, the snowmelt runoff contributed to the bridge failure closing the road sooner than anticipated.

An inch or less of slushy, wet snow led to a multiple-vehicle accident on US-41 near Teal Lake in Negaunee on the morning of the 6th at approximately 8 am. An eastbound vehicle driven by an Ishpeming man lost control on the slushy road and collided with a pickup truck in the westbound lane driven by a Negaunee man. The eastbound vehicle then struck another vehicle. The Ishpeming man sustained multiple serious injuries in the crash and was transported to UPHS in Marquette by ambulance for medical treatment. The Negaunee man sustained minor injuries and sought his own medical treatment. All vehicles involved in the crash were disabled and towed from the scene. The Negaunee Police Department was assisted by Michigan State Police, the Negaunee Fire Department, Bell EMS and Marquette County Rescue units. The highway was closed for approximately one hour on the morning of the 6th.

Wide ranging storm total snow amounts were reported across the county during the blizzard event.  Snow amounts ranged from 4 to 7 inches near Lake Superior to as much as two to nearly three feet of snow over the higher terrain of western Marquette County. The Ishpeming and National Mine areas received the most snow with anywhere from 27 to 33 inches of storm total snow while the NWS Marquette office measured 24.4 inches.  North to northeast winds gusting over 50 mph at times also caused blizzard conditions in snow and blowing snow throughout much of the 13th.  The heavy snow also resulted in minor accidents and vehicles getting stranded on the 13th.
Significant storm total lake effect snowfall amounts during the event included nearly three feet of snow at Mount Arvon, 19 inches at Herman and 11 inches just south of Baraga.

Two-day storm total lake effect snowfall across Alger County ranged from 8 to 12 inches along the Lake Superior shoreline to as much as 18 to 24 inches over higher terrain areas south of Munising and Grand Marais.  North winds gusting as high as 45 mph also resulted in near-blizzard conditions at times in snow and blowing snow.

A fairly widespread 10 to 14 inches of very wet, heavy lake enhanced snow occurred over the higher terrain areas of Marquette County away from Lake Superior from the evening of the 2nd into the early evening of the 3rd.  North to northeast winds gusting near 50 mph caused blizzard conditions at times, especially on the morning of the 3rd, and along with the wet snow resulted in tree damage and widespread power outages.  Schools were closed through the county on the 3rd, including Northern Michigan University.

Observed snowfall over an approximate 36-hour time period included 28 inches at Herman, 16.5 inches near Three Lakes and 10 inches around the Baraga area.  The heavy wet snow combined with winds gusting over 40 mph at times caused tree damage, power outages and closed several schools in the county on the 3rd.

Observers reported widespread heavy snow of 6 to 9 inches across the county in less than a 24-hour period.  The wet heavy snow combined with north-northeast wind gusts to around 50 mph at times caused tree damage, knocked out power for nearly 7500 customers, caused traffic accidents and closed schools throughout the county on the 3rd.  Menominee County 911 reported extremely dangerous road conditions and advised motorists not to travel unless absolutely necessary.

Observers reported widespread snow amounts of 4 to 6 inches across the county in an approximate 12-hour period.  The heavy wet snow combined with north wind gusts near 40 mph caused some tree damage and power outages while closing schools throughout the county on the 3rd.

Observers measured a widespread 4 to 6 inches of wet, heavy snow across southern Schoolcraft County in less than a 15-hour period.  The wet snow caused hazardous travel and knocked out power to nearly 500 customers while closing schools throughout the county on the 3rd.

Observers snowfall reports in less than 15 hours included 10 inches at Sundell and 6 inches at Munising.  The wet snow combined with northeast winds gusting to around 50 mph caused hazardous travel and knocked out power to nearly 1000 customers while closing schools throughout the county on the 3rd.

Observer reports of a widespread 3 to 7 inches of wet, heavy snow combined with north winds to 30 mph at times caused tree damage, power outages to more than 4100 customers and closed schools throughout the county on the 3rd.

Observers measured a widespread 3 to 7 inches of wet, heavy snow over an approximate 36-hour period.  The wet snow caused hazardous travel, some power outages and closed schools throughout the county on the 3rd.

Observers snowfall reports over an approximate 24-hour period included 9 inches at Bergland Dam, and 4 inches each at six miles north of Greenland and at Paulding.  The wet, heavy snow combined with north winds gusting near 40 mph at times caused hazardous travel, sporadic power outages and closed schools throughout the county on the 3rd.

Observers reported a widespread 3 to 5 inches of wet, heavy snow across the county  over an approximate 12-hour period.  The wet snow caused hazardous travel and closed schools throughout the county on the 3rd.

Observers reported a widespread 4 to 6 inches of wet snow across the county over less than a 30-hour period.  The heavy snow combined with northeast wind gusts to 45 mph caused some minor tree damage, sporadic power outages and hazardous travel.

A 14-year-old Toledo, OH boy drowned in Lake Superior on the 24th after being caught in a rip current at a beach near the Lake Superior State Forest Campground.  A 15-year-old was also caught in the rip current but was able to swim to the safety of shallow water.  The Coast Guard, Luce County Sheriff and Michigan DNR conservation officers conducted a search by boat and helicopter until dusk on the evening of the 24th , but waves of 4 to 5 feet at the time of the drowning hindered search and recovery efforts.  The search continued on the next day with additional aid from the Michigan State Police Dive and Drone Team until the victim's body was recovered that afternoon on the 25th.

An abnormally and record dry September into the first half of October with precipitation deficits of more than 3 inches led to the ignition of the Summit Lake Wildfire which was discovered on the evening of October 18th in the northwest corner of the McCormick Wilderness between Summit Lake and Evergreen Lake. The McCormick Wilderness is located in Baraga County, 12.5 miles north of Michigamme, MI. The wildfire grew rapidly from 5 acres on the morning of the 19th to 100 acres on the morning of the 20th. Difficult access for firefighters combined with an abundant mix of hardwood and conifer trees for fuel allowed the wildfire to expand over 300 acres by the 27th before a combination of snow and rain on the 31st led to its eventual containment by early November.  Through the efforts of Ottawa National Forest personnel and resources, a Michigan Interagency Type III Incident Management Team and aircraft personnel and resources the cost of fighting the wildfire was estimated at $1.3 million.  Additional wildfires across the U.P. through the month of October resulted in about $750,000 in damages.

Spring snowmelt and flooding have forced the DNR to the temporary emergency closure of Arfelin Lake boating access site in Marquette County until road repairs can be made. Culvert and the dirt access road have failed and water is moving swiftly. A pickup truck became stuck when a portion of the road collapsed.

A localized area of up to 4.2 inches of rainfall fell (per a public source in Pequaming) in a few hours between about 12:30 AM through about 5 AM, with the Baraga and L'Anse CWOP stations recording rain rates of a quarter to half inch of rain per 15 minutes and various stations recorded 1-2+ inch per hour rates. This sudden rainfall caused road overtopping and washouts in the communities of Keweenaw Bay, Baraga, L'Anse, and Pequaming as well as rural surrounding areas. Bus routes were rerouted and beaches were closed due to wastewater backups causing E. Coli and Fecal Coliform contamination. Many basements and private drives were flooded as well. Local rivers such as the Silver River reported up to a 5 foot increase in only a few hours.

Winds sustained over 30 mph for several hours with frequent gusts 50-60 mph over the Keweenaw Peninsula and snowfall of around a foot.  The Copper Harbor ASOS (KP59) peak gust was 62 mph.  Key Impacts: Very difficult to impossible travel.

There were blizzard conditions with frequent wind gusts of 40-55 mph and snowfall of 8-12 in Northern Houghton County. The Houghton ASOS (KCMX) peak gust was 55 mph. Isolated power outages. Key Impacts: Very difficult to impossible travel, power outages.

The Houghton ASOS (KCMX) peak gust was 60 mph and K.I. Sawyer ASOS (KSAW) peak gust was 53 mph before the wind sensor stopped reporting. Up to around 10% of customers without power. Key Impacts: Very difficult to impossible travel, power outages.

There were blizzard conditions with frequent wind gusts of 35-40 mph at NBDC Ontonagon and snowfall of 8-16 in Ontonagon County. Peak gust of 56mph at Ontonagon MDOT MC066. Key Impacts: Very difficult to impossible travel.

There were blizzard conditions with frequent wind gusts of 40-55 mph and snowfall of 8-12 in Marquette County. The K.I. Sawyer (KSAW) AWOS peak gust was 53 mph before the wind sensor stopped reporting. Widespread tree damage and power outages were reported, particularly near the lakeshore.  Some structures were damaged from trees falling on them. The Marquette Board of Light and Power reported (summarizing) the event rivaled anything in the past 10 to 20 years and the scale of damage, restoration and coordination was extraordinary. Up to 39% of customers were without power.  Some locations took up to 3 days to restore power.  Multiple warming shelters were opened. Road closures included M-28 due to whiteout conditions. Key Impacts: Very difficult to impossible travel, power outages, tree damage, structure damage, road closures.

Road closures included M-35 due to downed power lines.  Up to around 25% of customers without power.  Key Impacts: Very difficult to impossible travel, road closures, power outages.

There were blizzard conditions with frequent wind gusts of 40-55 mph and snowfall of 8-18 in Northern Schoolcraft County. The Munising ASOS (KP53) peak gust was 64 mph and the Newberry AWOS (KERY) reported a peak gust of 41 mph. Up to around 10% of customers without power.  Key Impacts: Very difficult to impossible travel, power outages.

High winds and heavy snow brought blizzard conditions to Luce County.  ERY ASOS reported blizzard conditions. Snowfall of over two feet fell across much of the county. Up to 10% of the county was without power during the event. Key impacts: school closures, power outages, impossible travel.

High winds and heavy snow brought blizzard conditions to Northern Schoolcraft County.  ISQ and ERY ASOS reported blizzard conditions. Snowfall of two to three feet fell across much of the county. Up to 20% of the county was without power during the event. A few FM radio towers became inoperable. Plowing operations suspended due to severe weather conditions. Hospital closed for non-essential services. Key impacts: school and hospital closures, power outages, impossible travel.

High winds and heavy snow brought blizzard conditions to Delta County.  ESC/MNM ASOS reported blizzard conditions. Snowfall of over two feet fell across much of the county. Up to 7% of the county was without power during the event. A few FM radio towers became inoperable. Plowing operations suspended due to severe weather conditions. MI Governor declared a state of emergency. Flights cancelled to/from ESC. Vehicles were reported stranded, especially in the Escanaba area.  A Local Area Emergency was issued by request from the EM for impassable roads and extreme travel conditions and to advise people to stay off the roads.  An elderly person had to be rescued from their home using snowmobiles and side-by-sides due to impassable roads after loosing power in the Garden Peninsula. Key impacts: school closures, power outages, impossible travel.

High winds and heavy snow brought blizzard conditions to Menominee County. MNM ASOS reported blizzard conditions. Snowfall of over two feet fell across much of the county. Up to 1% of the county was without power during the event. A few FM radio towers became inoperable. Plowing operations were suspended due to severe weather conditions and secondary roads were impassable. The Menominee County Sheriff's office advised the public not to travel. Key impacts: school closures, power outages, impossible travel.

High winds and heavy snow brought blizzard conditions to Marquette County. SAW ASOS reported blizzard conditions. Snowfall of two to four feet fell across much of the county. Up to 14% of the county was without power during the event. A few FM radio towers became inoperable. Plowing operations were suspended due to severe weather conditions and secondary roads were impassable. Portions of M-28 closed east of Kawbawgam Rd. The County Sheriff advised the public not to venture out on foot or by car. 19 carbon monoxide calls were received by dispatch along with 18 vent cleanouts. Vehicles were reported stranded in the Gwinn/Sawyer area. Cinder Pond Marina in Marquette's lower harbor had two piers heavily damaged by waves/ice. Key impacts: school closures, power outages, impossible travel.

High winds and heavy snow brought blizzard conditions to Alger County. SAW ASOS reported blizzard conditions. Snowfall of two to four feet fell across much of the county. The County Sheriff advised the public not to venture out on foot or by car. Key impacts: school closures, power outages, impossible travel.

Emergency management reported that the road into the Otter Lake Dam was completely submerged by 10 AM on the 18th. Trained spotters reported that the access to the wire weight gauge on the Sturgeon River at Chassell was impossible due to water over Sturgeon River Road. Damage was considered minimal and damage estimates are not available.

County emergency management reported 20 to 30 roads flooded by 9:45 AM on the 12th, with significant flooding of the US-2 rail underpass in Powers as well as much of the surrounding town and the nearby town of Wilson. On the 13th, railroad tracks in Faithorn were washed out. In the overnight of the 13th into the 14th, County Road 563 washed out at Wilson Creek. One water rescue was performed in Harris Township on the 14th.Due to the severity of the flooding, a Disaster Declaration Request was approved by the president on June 30th.

County emergency management reported Delta County Airport closed on the 13th due to water over the runways. Power was cut to the VOR facility and water was at least 3 feet deep. At least 4 roads in the city of Escanaba were closed on the 13th. In Rapid River, water over the road closed the US-41 and US-2 intersection. A culvert washout closed County Road 503 in Bay De Noc Township from the 16th to the 17th. Water over the road on County Road 497/GG in Nahma caused the road to be closed from the 17th to the 27th. Drone footage along the Ford River provided by the emergency manager highlighted multiple structures threated, surrounded, or inundated by high water. County emergency manager estimates private property damages around 300 Thousand $USD and the public damages at approximately 250 Thousand $USD.

County Road Commission reported that water over the road caused County Road 577 in Vulcan to be closed on the 15th. Video on social media showed a railroad track washout near Sagola on the 17th. Damage estimates were minimal and considered part of routine maintenance.

County emergency management reported that the M-69 bridge was closed on the 21st and advised residents to evacuate if they resided near flooded waters. On the 18th, social media reports showed inundation for low lying areas in the town of Amasa including damage to local parks and residential septic systems. Deer Lake became inaccessible due to road washouts on the 18th. Flooding in Sagola resulted in railroad washouts. Due to the severity of the flooding, a Disaster Declaration Request was approved by the president on June 30th.

Emergency management reported multiple rivers and low lying areas were inundated by the combination of rain and snowmelt. In Gwinn, multiple roadways were inaccessible due to flooding on the Escanaba River by the 18th. Division Street in Negaunee was closed daily from the 13th onwards. Harlow Lake Rd (County Road HD) was closed at County Road 550 on the 17th. Flooding at Pelissier Lake in Sands Township resulted in 1 evacuation with well water being unsafe due to the high water table making septic systems inoperable. Ely, Humboldt, Champion, and Republic townships experienced water over multiple roadways, including the road at Steel Bridge Rd (Ely Township, County Road CG) on the 18th. The Chocolay River Fishing pier was underwater by the 19th. The Iron Ore Heritage Trail west of Wawanowin Rd to the city of Republic had flowing water on the trail by the 21st. 10 properties along the Michigamme River were inaccessible on the 23rd. Jasper Street in Ishpeming had a sinkhole that was filled on the 23rd. Due to the severity of the flooding, a Disaster Declaration Request was approved by the president on June 30th.

A Negaunee man drowned while swimming near Picnic Rocks in Marquette at 4:34 pm on the 10th. A long shore current developing between the shore and rocks was believed to be a contributing factor in the drowning. The Marquette Coast Guard indicated a north wind of 10 to 15 knots with waves reported to be 3 to 5 feet at the time of the drowning.

The Pinery Wildfire started east of L���Anse on the 20th around 3:30pm local time and burned 685 acres before being contained on the 22nd. Human burning of debris and brush in the early afternoon of the 20th, strong southerly winds gusting as high as 50 mph, and very low relative humidity values of 15-25% caused and sustained the wildfire. The wildfire destroyed a mobile home and damaged the Pinery Ski Lake Cross Country Ski Trails and Pinery Cemetery. The fire fighting efforts were led by the Michigan DNR and BIA, which contained the fire on the 22nd and finished mop up on the 26th. The cost of fighting the fire was estimated at near $125,000. The total damage estimate is unknown at this time.

The Black River Falls Wildfire started southwest of Ishpeming in Marquette County on the afternoon of the 20th. The wildfire was ignited when a jack pine tree branch split off the main stem from strong southerly winds and fell across a power line. The wildfire burned 811 acres, destroyed 21 residences and 12 other structures. The fire fighting efforts were led by the Michigan DNR. The wildfire was contained on the 22nd and mop up efforts continued into the 26th.  The cost for personnel and equipment to fight the wildfire was estimated at near $100,000. The total damage estimate is unknown at this time but presumed to be in the millions of dollars.

A 40-foot by 70-foot section of the Fontana Terminal Building at the Ford Airport in Iron Mountain was torn off by winds exceeding 60 mph.  Two flights were cancelled due to the damage and the passengers were bused to Escanaba to catch alternate flights.

The Grapevine Wildfire started on the afternoon of the 29th and burned into the 31st.  The wildfire burned between 80 and 100 acres.  Numerous local fire departments responded and help suppress the fire around its edges.  Heavy equipment was also used to build up barriers around the fire.  No structures were lost in the fire.
A waterspout was observed for 15 to 20 seconds near the north shore of the Dead River Basin.
Nickle to quarter-sized hail was observed at the far west end of Big Manistique Lake just east of Germfask.

The spotter at the headquarters of Porcupine Mountains State Park reported severe downdrafts, trees falling, dime-sized hail, significant lightning and heavy rain and runoff for approximately 20 minutes.  Four large trees fell across roads, blocking lanes in the park.

A strong EF0 tornado with winds estimated around 85 mph touched down at the River Pines RV Park and Campground and then skipped northeastward across the village lifting on the east side of the Ontonagon Golf Course.  Most of the damage was confined to snapped and uprooted trees, snapped power poles, a small flipped boat, minor roof damage, and some structural damage to a garage.  There were no injuries.
An apple tree six inches in diameter was knocked down.  Various tree branches three inches in diameter were also down.  Hanging plants were blown off the porch.
Wind gusts were estimated at 30 mph from the storm.
Pea to penny-sized hail was also reported 3.5 miles south of Republic.
Eight to ten-inch diameter tree down on road.
About a dozen trees were uprooted and numerous branches broken in the Escanaba River State Forest along the Menominee River.
Peak wind gust measured at the Michigan Tech University Keweenaw Research Center.

Winds in the wake of a cold frontal passage gusted to 58 mph at Freda.
An awning was blown off of a business on Highway US-45 in Rockland.

The Keweenaw County Sheriff reported multiple large trees down across roads throughout Keweenaw County.  Power was out in Copper Harbor from 1545-2115 EDT.

Strong north winds from the storm knocked down numerous large trees across roads and power lines and caused widespread power outages across Marquette County from the evening of the 29th into the morning of the 30th.  Thousands of residences in Marquette, Harvey, Skandia, Negaunee, Ishpeming and Gwinn were without power from the evening of the 29th into the 30th.  Some customers were without power for several days.  The most extensive and widespread tree damage observed was on Partridge Bay Trail off of County Road 550 just northwest of Marquette where hundreds of one to two-foot diameter oak and quaking aspen trees were toppled across the road.  Heavy rain accompanying the storm also caused ponding of water on city streets.||In addition...bricks blown off the Pioneer Square Building in Ishpeming caused extensive damage to a pickup truck.
Several trees were knocked down and hundreds were without power across Houghton County into the morning of the 30th.
The West Iron County Fire Department reported power lines down from the storm while the Crystal Falls fire department observed a power outage.
Several 5 to 6-inch diameter poplar trees were knocked down in Iron Mountain.
The Alger County Sheriff reported numerous trees down across roads and power lines across the county. Several of the trees were greater than 12 inches in diameter.
Large trees fell across power lines just north of Menominee along Highway M-35.  Two to three-inch diameter tree limbs were also reported down over the south side of Menominee.

Several trees were reported down in the Escanaba and Gladstone area as tree branches fell across roads and power lines.  Over 100 customers in rural Escanaba and Gladstone were without power into the evening of the 30th.
Several trees were reported down in the Manistique area.

The National Weather Service in Negaunee Township measured 12.2 inches of wet heavy snow in less than 24 hours while the Ishpeming area measured around 10 inches.  In addition to numerous minor accidents, the combination of wet snow and north wind gusts to 35 mph caused power outages and sporadic tree damage throughout Marquette County. The storm closed schools in Ishpeming, Negaunee and Marquette on the 10th.
The observer near Herman measured 13.1 inches of snow in 18 hours.  The wet snow caused numerous minor accidents, sporadic power outages and some tree damage.

An estimated six inches of snow fell in less than 12 hours in Iron Mountain.  The combination of wet snow and north wind gusts to 30 mph caused numerous minor accidents and power outages across the area.

A spotter near Iron River measured nine inches of snow in less than 12 hours.  The wet heavy snow and north winds gusting to 30 mph caused numerous minor accidents, power outages and some tree damage.  West Iron County schools were closed on the 10th while Forest Park School had a two-hour delay.
Eight inches of snow fell in Sundell over an 11-hour period.

Two inches of wet slushy snow contributed to a fatal car crash near Rapid River at shortly before 430 pm on the afternoon of the 9th as reported by the Michigan State Police post in Gladstone.  Two elderly women from Rapid River were pronounced dead at the scene when the car they were driving slid out of control and was struck by an SUV driven by a 53-year-old Wisconsin man. The man was transported by ambulance to OSF St. Francis Hospital in Escanaba and was listed in fair condition the next day. Both vehicles were heavily damaged.||Several other accidents were reported in the Escanaba-Gladstone area with numerous calls of vehicles sliding into the ditch.

Around six inches of snow fell in a 24-hour period from Redridge to the Houghton-Hancock area.  The wet heavy snow and over 30 mph northerly wind gusts resulted in nine power outages in the Houghton area that affected more than 3500 residences.
Six inches of wet heavy snow fell northeast of Calumet in a 24-hour period.
A resident three miles east of Kenton measured 7.5 inches of storm total snowfall in less than 24 hours.
Seven to eight inches of snow fell in less than 24 hours near Wakefield and Watersmeet.
An estimated eight inches of snowfall was reported near Paulding in less than 24 hours.

Two inches of wet snow resulted in slick roadways across portions of southern Schoolcraft County on the afternoon and evening of the 9th.  The Schoolcraft County Sheriff reported three vehicular accidents due to the slippery roadways.
The observer near South Range measured 12.5 inches of lake effect snow in 30 hours.  An estimated eight inches of snow fell in Calumet over a 12-hour period ending on the morning of the 17th.
The spotter ten miles east of Ontonagon estimated four inches of snow over a 12-hour period.  Strong winds caused blowing snow all day.
The spotter at Two Heart measured 11.5 inches of lake effect snow over a 36-hour period.
Spotters measured six to seven inches of snow from Republic to Ishpeming.  Most of the snow fell in less than an eight-hour period.
Seven to eight inches of wet heavy snow fell from Sidnaw to Watton and Covington in less than a six-hour period with two-inch per hour snowfall rates reported at times.
Seven to nine inches of wet heavy snow fell in the Sidnaw area in less than an eight-hour period.  Snowfall rates of two inches per hour were reported at times.

Spotters in and near Ironwood measured anywhere from 11 to 14 inches of wet heavy snow over a ten-hour time period.  The spotter just northwest of Ironwood reported snowfall rates of two to three inches per hour at times.   The Wakefield area reported over one-inch per hour snowfall rates during the event.
A swath of ten inches of wet heavy snow fell from White Pine to Rockland in an eight-hour period.
The spotter near Winona measured eight inches of wet heavy snow in a 12-hour period.

The spotter nine miles southwest of Big Bay measured seven inches of wet heavy snow in a 14-hour period.  Five to six inches of snow were also reported from Negaunee to Ishpeming.  Sporadic power outages were reported due to the heavy wet snow.
The spotter near Ironwood measured 6.5 inches of wet heavy snow in 12 hours.  An estimated eight inches of snow fell near Lake Gogebic State Park in about a 12-hour period.
A fairly widespread 7 to 8 inches of wet heavy snow fell over a 12-hour period across much of Ontonagon County.
Spotters near Twin Lakes, Chassell, Jacobsville, Houghton and Calumet measured a widespread 7 to 8 inches of wet, heavy snow in a 12-hour period.
Spotters from Calumet to Mohawk measured 6 to 7 inches of wet heavy snow in 12 hours.
Spotters at Herman and near Sidnaw measured five inches of wet heavy snow in just over 12 hours. Several accidents were reported in the L'anse area due to slippery roads.
A spotter near Sidnaw measured five inches of wet heavy snow in just over 12 hours.
A spotter near Iron River measured 5.5 inches of snow in just over 12 hours.

The spotter near Toivola estimated 12 inches of lake effect snow fell in a 12-hour period ending on the morning of the 9th.  A public report from Twin Lakes measured 10 to 11 inches of snow in 24 hours.
Observers in Grand Marais measured nine to ten inches of lake effect snow in a 6-hour period.  Near blizzard conditions in blowing snow were also reported as west winds gusted to around 35 mph.
A public report from the town of Gay estimated 7 to 8 inches of lake effect snow over a 12-hour period.

Slippery roadways caused by an inch of lake effect snow moving through the area resulted in at least four accidents around the Marquette area on the morning of the 8th.  Three of the accidents occurred along Highway M-553, the most serious of which occurred just south of Marquette Mountain at around 7 am.  This two-car crash resulted in injuries to the driver and two passengers of the northbound vehicle which lost control and collided with the southbound vehicle.  All three people were transported to Marquette General Hospital.  A fourth accident occurred near Shiras Hills in Marquette.

A slushy mixture of rain and snow contributed to a fatal accident on US Highway 45 near Bruce Crossing at 11 am on the morning of the 14th.  Michigan State Police in Wakefield reported that a 36 year-old Michigan Tech University student from St. Paul, MN was killed when the vehicle he was driving spun head-on into the path of a semi-tractor and trailer rig driven by a Greenland man.  The Greenland man received minor injuries in the accident according to police reports.

Slippery roads from several inches of lake effect snow contributed to numerous car   accidents from Ironwood through Wakefield to Marenisco on the 16th.  One two-car accident in Bessemer resulted in injuries to a 44 year-old man.
A spotter in Harvey measured five inches of lake effect snow in three and a half hours late on the 22nd.

A spotter near Chatham measured 5.5 inches of lake effect snow in five hours late on the 22nd.  The observer south of Grand Marais also reported over five inches of snow in the 12-hour period ending on the morning of the 23rd.
An estimated four to six inches of snow fell near Copper Harbor in a nine-hour period on the 29th.

A quick inch of wet snow created slippery roads and contributed to a fatal accident just south of Marquette Mountain on Highway M-553 around 10 am on the 29th.  A 26 year-old Gwinn man was killed when the northbound car he was driving spun out of  control and crashed into a garbage truck heading southbound.  The six-month old daughter of the Gwinn man was injured in the crash and transported to Marquette General Hospital. She was listed in stable condition the next day. The driver of the garbage truck was not injured.

Spotters north of Calumet measured 4 to 8 inches of snow in 12 hours while northwest winds gusting at or above 40 mph caused occasional blizzard conditions in blowing snow from late on the 1st into the morning of the 2nd.
A spotter near the Bergland Dam measured a storm total of 13 inches of snowfall.
The spotter at Painesdale measured a storm total snowfall of 17 inches.

A spotter at Ironwood measured 17 inches of storm total snowfall while a report from Wakefield measured over a foot of snow.  Northwest winds gusting to 35 mph also resulted in considerable blowing and drifting of snow during the event.
The observer in Herman measured 8.4 inches of snow in 24 hours.

The Marquette area received an estimated 11 inches of snow in ten hours on the morning of the 2nd.  The observer northwest of Ishpeming measured 11 inches of snow in the 24-hour period ending on the morning of the 2nd.
Lake effect snow accumulation of 4 to 8 inches from Munising to Grand Marais combined with northwest winds gusting over 40 mph produced blizzard conditions over a 24-hour time period.

Widespread lake effect snow accumulation of 2 to 4 inches from Eben Junction to Grand Marais combined with northwest winds gusting near 40 mph produced considerable  drifting and blowing snow and near whiteout conditions at times.

An estimated 10 to 12 inches of lake effect snow fell across the area over a 24-hour period.  Occasional northwest winds gusts to 30 mph also produced considerable blowing and drifting of snow and reduced visibility.

Eight to ten inches fell across the area over a 24-hour period.  Northwest winds gusting to 35 mph produced considerable blowing and drifting of snow and reduced visibility along the Lake Superior shoreline.
Spotter reports from 12 miles east of Steuben to near Manistique measured 10 to 14 inches of lake effect snow in less than a 24-hour period.

Four inches of moderate lake effect snow fell in six hours at Rockland.

The trained spotter four miles northeast of Calumet measured 12.5 inches of lake effect snow in 28 hours.  The snow combined with north winds gusting to 30 mph produced considerable blowing snow and reduced visibility to one half mile or less at times from the morning of the 12th into the early afternoon of the 13th.

Trained spotters in the Calumet area measured over a foot of snow in 24 hours. The snow combined with north winds gusting to 30 mph produced considerable blowing snow and reduced visibility to one half mile or less at times from the morning of the 12th into the afternoon of the 13th.

A spotter near Mass City measured an estimated 10 to 12 inches of lake effect snow in 24 hours.  Sustained northwest winds of 20 mph with gusts near 30 mph also produced considerable blowing snow and reduced visibility of one half mile or less.
The Gogebic County Sheriff estimated that a foot of lake effect snow fell in 12 hours at Bessemer during the event.  Spotters at Marenisco and Ironwood measured 11 inches of snow during the event.
The spotter at Herman measured 13.5 inches of lake effect snow in 24 hours.  Northwest wind gusting to 25 mph at times also caused some blowing and drifting of snow during the event.

A spotter in Ishpeming measured ten inches of lake effect snow in 24 hours.  Northwest winds gusting to 30 mph caused reduced visibility of less than one half mile at times and made measuring of snow difficult due to drifting.
The spotter near Silver City estimated 8 to 10 inches of lake effect snow during the event.

A spotter in Ironwood estimated eight inches of lake effect snow fell in less than 12 hours.  One inch per hour snowfall rates were reported between 4 am and 11 am.  Several car accidents were attributed to the snow and blowing snow from the storm.

At the National Weather Service in Negaunee Township, seven inches of snow fell in 12 hours with one-inch per hour snowfall rates between 7 am and 1 pm.  Northwest winds gusting near 30 mph also caused considerable blowing and drifting of snow.

Spotters near Munising and Christmas reported over one-inch per hour snowfall rates at times between 10 am and 5 pm.  The observer near Munising measured nine inches of snow in less than 24 hours during the event.  North winds gusting over 30 mph also resulted in considerable blowing and drifting of snow.
The spotter in Herman measured seven inches of lake effect snow during the event.

Observers measured anywhere from 3 to 6 inches across the northern portion of the county.  Northwest winds gusting near 30 mph at times also caused considerable blowing of snow reducing visibility to one half mile or less at times.

The spotter four miles east of Silver City measured 11 inches of snow during the event.  Most of the snow fell by 6 pm on the 19th.  Frequent blowing snow and whiteout conditions were reported on the 19th.

Trained spotters between Calumet and Delaware measured 5 to 6 inches of lake effect snow from the evening of the 19th into the morning of the 20th.  Northwest winds gusting over 30 mph frequently reduced visibility to one half mile or less in blowing snow on the 19th.

Observers from Winona to Painesdale and Redridge measured around a foot of snow during the event.  Northwest winds gusting near 30 mph also reduced visibility to one half mile or less in blowing snow on the 19th.

There was a report of an estimated five inches of snowfall in eight hours at Melstrand during the day on the 19th.  Northwest winds gusting over 30 mph also reduced visibility to one half mile or less in blowing snow on the 19th.

There was a report of four inches of snow ten miles east of Steuben in a six hour period.  The snow combined with northwest winds gusting over 30 mph also reduced visibility to one half mile or less in blowing snow on the 19th.
The observer northeast of Iron Mountain measured .20 of an inch of ice accumulation from freezing rain early morning on the 23rd.  Schools were closed through the county on the 23rd due to the storm.

The observer in Menominee measured one-eighth of an inch of ice accumulation from freezing rain on the 23rd.  Side roads were covered in ice which resulted in several cars sliding into the ditch.  Many area schools were closed on the 23rd due to the icy roads.

Observers near Gladstone and Bark River measured around .15 of an inch of ice accumulation from freezing rain. The ice on roadways caused numerous accidents, three of which resulted in minor injuries. Area schools were cancelled on the 23rd due to the storm.

Six inches of wet heavy snow fell in six hours at the National Weather Service in Negaunee Township on the 23rd.  Over one-inch per hour snowfall rates were also reported near Big Bay and Ishpeming along with a light glaze of ice accumulation from freezing drizzle. Area schools including Northern Michigan University were closed on the 23rd due to the storm.

Observers eight miles west of Ontonagon and in White Pine and Paulding measured 6 to 7 inches of snow in eight hours on the 23rd.  Some light glaze of ice accumulation was also reported due to freezing drizzle.
The spotter east of Watersmeet measured eight inches of wet snow in 12 hours.

The spotter four miles northeast of Calumet measured over seven inches of wet snow in 12 hours while the observer in Mohawk measured over 11 inches of snow in a 24-hour period ending on the morning of the 24th.

Spotters from Calumet to Hancock measured 7 to 8 inches of wet snow in a 12-hour period.  Storm total snow accumulation into the morning of the 24th exceeded a foot at Twin Lakes, Calumet and Hancock.
An estimated eight inches of wet snow fell in Kenton on the morning of the 23rd.
Seven inches of wet snow fell in L'anse on the morning of the 23rd. A 24-hour storm total of 11 inches fell in Herman ending on the morning of the 24th.
The observer just east of Stambaugh measured eight inches of wet snow in just over 12 hours.

The observer ten miles east of Ontonagon estimated eight inches of snow in less than 12 hours.  Northwest winds gusting over 30 mph also caused significant blowing of snow with whiteout conditions on roadways.
The observer near Winona measured 12 inches of snow in 24 hours.

The Houghton County Sheriff estimated 11 inches of snow fell at Alston in less than 10 hours on the 28th.  There was a 24-hour snowfall total of 11 inches from Pelkie ending on the morning of the 29th.  Three inch per hour snowfall rates were reported at times in Pelkie.
The spotter in Melstrand estimated 12 inches of snow in 24 hours.
The spotter at Pine Stump Junction measured 14 inches of snow in less than 24 hours.
An estimated 12 inches of storm total snowfall occurred along the northern Schoolcraft and Alger County line.
Ten inches of snow fell in 12 hours in L'anse during the day on the 28th, and a 24-hour storm total snowfall of 17 inches was measured at Herman ending on the morning of the 29th.
The observer near Big Bay measured 8.5 inches of snow in 24 hours.

Slippery roads from an inch of wet snow resulted in several accidents in the southern part of the county.  Several vehicles slid into the ditch in the Iron Mountain and Norway areas.  ||Two semi-trucks collided on US-2 at Lake Antoine Road in Iron Mountain.  One truck was a logging truck and the collision spilled logs onto the roadway disabling both vehicles.  No injuries were reported from the the crash, but both trucks had to be towed from the scene.  It took two hours for the logs to be cleared off the road.
A band of moderate snow showers dropped three to four inches of wet snow from near Silver City south to Bergland on the morning of the 2nd.
Over six inches of lake effect snow fell in a 12-hour period at the National Weather Service in Negaunee Township.
There was a public report of five inches of lake effect snow accumulation in L'anse in a nine-hour period.
Spotters reported four inches of lake effect snow from White Pine to Silver City in a 12-hour period.  Snow and blowing snow reduced visibility to one half mile at times.
Spotters from Eben Junction to Munising reported three to four inches of snow along with considerable blowing and drifting of snow.  Visibility was reduced to one half mile or less at times.
The observer in Laurium measured eight inches of lake enhanced snow in 12 hours.
Total lake effect snow accumulation between Bessemer and Ironwood measured from seven to nine inches with one-inch per hour snowfall rates recorded.
The observer eight miles west of Ontonagon measured 15 inches of lake effect snow in less than 24 hours with one-inch per hour snowfall rates reported.
There was a public report of seven inches of lake effect snow in 16 hours eight miles southwest of Munising.

The observer four miles northeast of Calumet measured 13 inches of lake effect snow in less than 24 hours.  Easterly winds gusting to 35 mph also produced considerable blowing and drifting of snow and reduced visibility to one-quarter mile or less at times.

Twenty-four hour storm total snowfall amounts over northern Houghton included 13 inches at Redridge and around 12 inches at Hancock and Calumet.  Easterly winds gusting to 35 mph also caused considerable blowing and drifting of snow reducing visibility to one-quarter mile at times.
The observer four miles east of Silver City measured 9.5 inches of lake effect snow in 24 hours.

Storm total snowfall across the county included 14.5 inches near Marenisco, an estimated 13 inches at Bessemer and 10 inches in 12 hours just west of Watersmeet.  East wind gusting near 30 mph at times also caused considerable blowing and drifting of snow. Many area schools were closed due to the storm.
The spotter just south of Iron River measured 19 inches of storm total snowfall.  Many area schools were closed due to the storm.

Storm total snowfall amounts included 17 inches at Norway and 16 inches at Iron Mountain.  East wind gusting near 25 mph at times also caused some blowing and drifting of snow.  Most schools were closed due to the storm.

Storm total snowfall amounts included 15 inches at Daggett, 13 inches at Carney and 9 inches at Menominee.  East winds gusting near 30 mph at times also caused considerable blowing and drifting of snow.  The winter storm prompted county officials to declare an unprecedented snow emergency to urge people to stay off area highways. The Menominee County Courthouse and area schools were closed.
The spotter near Covington estimated five to six inches of snowfall in less than five hours.

Snowfall amounts included eight inches in less than five hours at Arnold, eight to nine inches in 12 hours near Ishpeming, and seven inches in ten hours near Negaunee. East winds gusting over 25 mph at times also caused considerable blowing and drifting of snow.  Most schools throughout the county closed due to the storm.

Spotters in Bark River and Escanaba estimated 12 inches of snow in nine hours while Gladstone reported nine inches in six hours.  East winds gusting over 30 mph also caused considerable blowing and drifting of snow.  Many area schools were closed due to the storm.
The spotter in Bruce Crossing measured nearly six inches of snow in six hours.
The spotter near Sidnaw measured eight inches of snow in seven hours.

The observer in Mohawk measured 7.2 inches of snow in eight hours with four inches occurring between 3 and 5 pm.  East winds gusting to near 40 mph at times also caused considerable blowing and drifting of snow and near whiteout conditions.

The spotter in Hancock measured 11.5 inches of snow in 14 hours.  East winds gusting near 40 mph at times also caused considerable blowing and drifting of snow as reported by the Houghton County Sheriff.
Spotters near Wetmore measured seven to eight inches of snow in five hours.
The spotter in Newberry estimated four to five inches of snow in approximately three hours.
An estimated six inches of snow fell in ten hours near Steuben.
An estimated six inches of snow fell in less than 12 hours over northern Schoolcraft County.
A spotter near Menominee measured four inches of wet snow in 12 hours.

The spotter near Round Lake measured six inches of wet snow in the 12-hour period ending on the morning of the 3rd.  The Escanaba-Gladstone area received four to five inches of snow during the same time frame with a number of accidents reported by the Delta County Sheriff.
Spotters in the Newberry area measured seven to eight inches of wet snow in 12 hours.

Storm total snowfall ending on the morning of the 4th included 24 inches near Shingleton and over 20 inches near Chatham and Munising.  Snow fell over approximately a 36-hour period. North winds gusting to 40 mph also caused areas of blowing and drifting snow near Lake Superior.
An estimated six to eight inches of snow fell in 12 hours over northern Schoolcraft County based on nearby spotter reports.
The spotter near Manistique measured six inches of wet snow in 12 hours.

Storm total snowfall amounts over a 36-hour period ending on the morning of the 4th included 27.4 inches northeast of Ishpeming, 24.5 inches in Negaunee, and an estimated 27 inches at Little Lake.  North winds gusting near 40 mph at times caused considerable blowing and drifting of snow especially along Lake Superior.

The observer in Herman measured 12.5 inches of storm total snowfall in less than 24 hours.  A spotter in L'anse also reported six inches of snow in six hours on the morning of the 3rd along with blowing and drifting snow.
The spotter just northeast of Calumet measured over 10 inches of storm total snowfall.
There was an public report of nine inches of snow measured in Calumet over a 26-hour period.
There was a public report of six inches of snow in less than 24 hours at White Pine.  3.7 inches of snow fell during a six-hour period on the 3rd.

Spotters in Marenisco and Wakefield measured four to five inches of snow over a five-hour period.  Northwest winds gusting at or above 30 mph also caused considerable blowing of snow and reduced visibility.
The observer near Chassell reported mainly pea-sized hailstones to a depth of one-half inch.  Some of the stones were dime-sized.
There was a public report in Calumet of nearly one-quarter inch of ice accumulation from freezing rain.
The observer in Herman measured two-tenths of an inch of ice accumulation from freezing rain.  The power was also knocked out at his residence.

South winds gusted between 50 and 60 mph at times from late morning into early afternoon.  The strong winds did minor damage and downed several trees between 9 and 12 inches in diameter in the city of Marquette.  The winds also downed two large maple trees in Skandia.
The observer in Herman measured 5.6 inches of wet snow in less than 24 hours.
Hail lasted five minutes.
Gusts up to 40 mph were reported with the storm.
Winds estimated at 60 mph knocked over a 24-inch diameter white pine tree six miles south of Witch Lake.
Trees were knocked down across Highway M-95 along the Marquette/Dickinson County line.
Very strong winds knocked down small tree limbs and blew patio furniture across the yard.
Hail was reported near the Sawyer Airport.
Hail was reported near Shot Point along Highway M-28.

The observer ten miles east of Ontonagon measured 1.75 inches of total rainfall.  A small creek on the residence was reported over its banks.  The observer at Rockland measured 2.80 inches of storm total rainfall.
Several trees were knocked down along County Road 581.

Lightning from a line of thunderstorms ignited The Duck Lake Wildfire 14 miles north of Newberry on the evening of the 20th. Strong south winds gusting over 30 mph on the 24th quickly fanned the fire and caused it to spread rapidly toward the Lake Superior shore forcing mandatory evacuations for people in the Pike Lake, Bodi Lake, Culhane Lake and Little Lake Harbor areas. The 21,069 acre wildfire, the third largest in modern Michigan history, burned 136 structures (including one store and one motel) before it was fully contained in mid-June. No injuries or deaths occurred from the fire. Road closures included County Road 414 east from the intersection with County Road 410 and County Road 500 from M-123 north to Little Lake Harbor. As a precaution, Tahquamenon Falls State Park was also closed for several days but was completely untouched by the fire. The total cost of property lost and resources used to fight the fire was estimated to be over $10 million. Governor Rick Snyder declared a state of disaster in Luce County on the 25th.

Lightning from thunderstorms ignited the Pine Creek North Wildfire on the evening of the 20th.  The fire spread to 3500 acres by the 25th but was 95 percent contained by the 28th.  The Marshland Wildlife Drive, Fishing Loop, Pine Ridge Nature Trail and many interior roads within the refuge were all closed due to the fire.  The cost of resources to fight the fire was estimated to be around $600,000.  No injuries or deaths were reported from the fire.  Governor Rick Snyder declared a state of disaster in Schoolcraft County on the 25th.

A lightning strike from thunderstorms caused a house fire in Iron Mountain on the evening of the 20th.  The home sustained damage in numerous areas, but firefighters were able to keep the damage contained to the second floor and attic.  The Iron Mountain Police Department, Beacon Ambulance and Wisconsin Electric were also at the scene of the fire to assist.
Lightning and high wind from thunderstorms caused more than 200 customers to lose power in Ishpeming.
Strong south winds ahead of a cold front caused downed power lines and knocked out power to more than 1200 customers in Munising.

The Department of Highways reported multiple trees down across Marquette County due to the high winds.  The high winds toppled large trees in Marquette and Harvey and also ripped siding off a building at Sawyer.
The spotter near Schaeffer reported trees greater than five inches in diameter down across his yard.
Power lines and trees were reported down across the railroad tracks in Menominee.  Emergency services were activated for the area.
The spotter seven miles southwest of Munising measured 1.50 inches of rain from a thunderstorm in 40 minutes.

Within the area of strongest wind damage several of the large trees fell on houses and vehicles and knocked down power poles and power lines. The NWS storm survey concluded that damage in and immediately surrounding Wakefield was caused by straight-line thunderstorm winds up to 90 mph.  Wind damage included an overturned camper trailer, a roof ripped off an old skating rink, a few damaged or destroyed outbuildings, hundreds of large uprooted or snapped trees (some 30 to 40 inches in diameter), downed power lines, and several trees downed on houses or vehicles.  The survey team could not access all areas around Wakefield due to the number of downed trees.  The time of the report was based on radar, observations and interviews of individuals in the area.

The NWS storm survey confirmed a low end EF1 tornado about three miles south of Bessemer.  Winds from the tornado were estimated around 90 mph.  The tornado touched down near the intersection of S. Barber Road and Spruce Road and ended 2.4 miles to the east-northeast, just northeast of the intersection of W. Harding Road and Koski Road.  Damage included multiple trees down on a garage on Spruce Street and  half a barn destroyed in Bessemer Township on Elder Street.  |||The damage path was 200 yards wide or less and occurred just before midnight CDT.

Portions of US Highway 41 and Highway M-94 were closed due to washouts or water over the road.  Green Garden Road and Magnum Road were also closed due to flooding. Water rescues were performed by firefighters and EMS personnel on Green Garden Road where water levels rose three to four feet into some homes. Ten people and four pets were rescued from the flood waters. ||In addition, flood water was also reported over Highway M-35 near County Road MU south of Richmond Township and basement flooding was reported in the Gwinn area. ||Damage from the flooding was estimated near 1.9 million dollars across Marquette County.

The driver and lone occupant of the vehicle lost control of his vehicle on County Road 416 in Cornell due to the slippery roads.  The vehicle left the roadway and collided with several trees on the east side of the road.

The Houghton County Sheriff reported a fatal two-vehicle accident on Highway M-26 near Dollar Bay on the morning of the 8th.  It is believed that several inches of lake effect snow caused the slippery conditions which contributed to the accident.  ||A 2002 Honda Accord collided head-on with a 2005 Chevy pickup truck around 750 am on M-26 near Coal Dock Road in Franklin Township.  The 21-year-old male driver of the Honda Accord was ejected and sustained fatal injuries in the crash.  The driver's 21-year old wife was also ejected during the crash and was in critical condition with multiple injuries.  The pickup driver and two other passengers in the pickup also sustained injuries.  The pickup driver's wife sustained serious injuries and was transported to U.P. Health System in Marquette.  A third passenger in the pickup, a six-year-old boy properly restrained in a child safety seat, escaped injury.

Lake effect snow and poor visibility contributed to a fatal car accident which occurred on US-2 near Gulliver on the early morning of the 3rd.  A semi-truck was westbound and a pickup truck was eastbound when one of the drivers lost control and the vehicles collided on US-2 west of Jackson Road in Doyle Township around 230 am.  The passenger of the pickup truck was pronounced dead at the scene of the accident.  The driver of the pickup truck was injured and taken to U.P. Health Systems in Marquette.  Two people in the semi-truck were taken to Schoolcraft Memorial Hospital for treatment.

Gusty westerly winds during the period which reached a peak gust of 58 mph at the Ironwood AWOS caused widespread power outages across the county as reported by WE Energies.  ||The strong wind gusts also uprooted and snapped large spruce trees in Marenisco on the evening of the 7th. The combination of three to four inches of lake effect snow and west winds gusting as high as 50 mph resulted in occasional whiteout conditions at several locations throughout the county.  ||The harsh winter weather and whiteout conditions led to a three vehicle accident on Highway US-41 by Canyon Falls at around 8:30 pm EST.  According to the Baraga County Sheriff's Department, two cars hit head-on and then one of the cars was hit by a semi-truck.   One of the drivers had to be extricated from the car by the jaws of life and sustained several spinal cord injuries.  Two children also sustained spinal cord injuries and were eventually air-lifted to the University Hospital in Ann Arbor the next afternoon.  The driver of the other car and a passenger in his vehicle sought their own medical treatment, and the driver of the semi-truck driver was uninjured.

At least two individuals were swimming in Lake Superior at a beach in Alger County, east of the Laughing Whitefish River outlet, when they were both swept out towards the open waters by a rip current. Both individuals were in water that was waist deep when the first individual was pulled out by the rip current. Upon trying to rescue the individual, the second swimmer was also pulled out by the same current. The current was so strong it was reported that the individual who lost their life had been ripped out of the hands of the second individual. The second individual was able to self-rescue back to shore, but unfortunately the first individual that was pulled out by the rip current was unreachable and lost their life. Extensive lake shore flooding was reported along Lake Superior from Marquette to Shot Point from north storm force winds building waves as high as 25 to 30 feet.  Two people drowned when they were swept off Black Rocks at Presque Isle Park in Marquette during the storm.   A U.S. Coast Guard helicopter from Air Station Traverse City flew in for a search and rescue operation but the victims were not found in the turbulent waters.   The storm and wave action did an estimated $500,000 in damage at Picnic Rocks Park along Lakeshore Boulevard in Marquette.

Winds gusting at or above 60 mph at times downed trees, power poles and power lines across much of the county on the 24th.  Au Train-Onoto and Munising public schools were closed on the 24th due the intense fall storm.

Three to nearly seven inches of rainfall in the early morning hours of the 17th caused widespread and catastrophic flash flooding across much of Houghton County from Chassell through Houghton/Hancock to Dollar Bay, Hubbell and Lake Linden.  The NOAA Precipitation Frequency Atlas indicated a 1000-year recurrence interval for rainfall  amounts of the magnitude which occurred during this event. The Houghton County emergency manager reported that nearly all roads were impassable in central and southern Houghton County. Many homes and businesses were flooded throughout the area, particularly in Houghton/Hancock where one fatality occurred when a basement collapsed at a home on Canal Road.  The Administration Building at Michigan Tech University also sustained flood damage. Governor Rick Snyder declared a state of disaster for Houghton County a day after the flooding occurred and damage estimates from flooding are currently over $100 million. Recovery efforts will be ongoing over Houghton County for the next several months.

Spotters reported between four to six inches of heavy wet snow during the late afternoon and evening hours across northern Houghton County.  Snowfall rates of an inch per hour or greater combined with east winds gusting to 45 mph caused near whiteout conditions and power outages from late afternoon into the early morning of the 12th.  Schools through the county were closed on the 12th due to impacts from the storm.

Between four and eight inches of wet snow fell over much of Menominee County during the event.  Sleet mixed in with the snow at times. East winds gusting over 30 mph at times also caused considerable blowing and drifting of snow as well.  Many schools throughout the county were closed on the 12th due to impacts from the storm.

There was an estimated four to six inches of wet snow over approximately 9 hours. Sleet likely mixed in with the snow at times.  East winds gusting to 40 mph also caused near whiteout conditions at times in snow and blowing snow and power outages during the evening of the 11th.  Many area schools were closed on the 12th due to impacts from the storm.
Spotters measured between four and seven inches of wet snow in approximately 10 hours.  Area schools were closed on the 12th due to impacts from the storm.

The spotter at Marenisco measured nearly six inches of wet snow in less than ten hours.  Sleet also mixed in with the snow at times.  A few schools had delayed start times on the 12th due to impacts from the storm.
A mix of wet snow and sleet accumulated from three to six inches over much of Iron County on the 11th.  West Iron County Schools were closed on the 12th to impacts from the storm.

There was an estimated four to six inches of wet snow in less than ten hours across the county.  Sleet mixed in with the snow at times.  Area schools were closed on the 12th due to impacts from the storm.

Spotter reports throughout the county measured anywhere from three to six inches of wet snow over an approximate 10-hour time period.  Marquette Board of Light and Power reported scattered power outages from the wet snow, and area schools were closed throughout the county on the 12th due to impacts from the storm.
There was a public report of two to three inches of wet heavy snow in less than five hours in Escanaba.  Scattered power outages were reported due to the heavy snow.

Freezing rain accumulated between one to two tenths of an inch of ice in Newberry from late evening on the 11th through the early morning of the 12th.  The freezing rain and east winds gusting over 30 mph at times caused scattered power outages over the county. The freezing rain also mixed with snow and sleet at times on the morning of the 12th. Tahquamenon Area Schools were delayed two hours on the 12th due to the impacts from the mixed precipitation and gusty winds.
Abundant and wet snow pack along with moderate rainfall at times contributed to minor flooding along the Sturgeon River from the 8th into early on the 13th.

Abundant and anomalously wet snow pack along with periods of moderate to heavy rain contributed to widespread minor flooding along the Sturgeon River from the 18th through the end of the month.  ||The Houghton County emergency manager reported that several houses and barns near the Sturgeon River at Chassell had rising water around them but no structures were inundated.  Sturgeon River Road was reported to be under 6-8 inches of water and Rajala Road was under 8-10 inches of water.  Multiple sections of Halonen Road near Pelkie and adjacent fields were reported to be under water the morning of 04/23 as the Sturgeon River crested.  Rain and snow melt runoff along with some clogged culverts led to Highway M-26 being closed south of Hubbell on the night of the 22nd due to water over the road.
Gages Creek overflowed its banks onto private property east of Peavy Pond on April 19th.  Minor flooding was also reported on the Paint and Michigamme Rivers from the 23rd into the 26th.
On the 20th, the Big Cedar River near Powers was inundating yards up near a few porches.  Other minor roads in Menominee County were reportedly under some water during this time.
Willow Creek in Escanaba spilled over onto Willow Creek Road on the 20th.

Norrie Park Road in Ironwood between Lime Street and Riverside Road was closed on the 22nd due to the failure of a small, old dam on the Montreal River.  Water was also reported over Black River Road near McDonald Dam on April 22.  On April 24th, numerous road closures were reported in the City of Wakefield as the Little Black River and Sunday Lake rose outside their banks. The city enlisted students to fill and place sandbags around the city.

Abundant wet snow pack combined with moderate to heavy rain at times caused minor flooding along the Michigamme River near Republic and Witch Lake and along the Middle Branch of the Escanaba near Humboldt from 23rd through the end of the month.  Some minor flooding was also reported along the Chocolay River near Harvey from the 18th through the 19th.
Minor flooding occurred into Dickinson County along the Michigamme River from the 23rd through the end of the month.

The observer in Mohawk reported visibility less than 500 feet in lake effect snow and blowing snow through much of the period.  The Houghton County Airport, ten miles to the southwest, reported frequent wind gusts greater than 40 mph with even a few gusts over 50 mph as wind chills lowered to 30 below to 40 below zero on the 10th. Highway 41 was closed from Delaware to Copper Harbor until early on the 11th due to the blizzard conditions which resulted in two-hour delays for area schools. Four to six inches of snow were reported during the blizzard event.

The ASOS at Houghton County Airport reported visibility less than one quarter mile in lake effect snow and blowing snow through much of the blizzard event as winds gusted over 50 miles at times.  Wind chills also lowered to 30 below to 40 below zero on the 10th.  Road closures from the blizzard continued into the 11th and caused two-hour delays in school start times. Four to six inches of snow were observed during the blizzard event.

The Rockland observer reported whiteout conditions in lake effect snow and blowing snow as winds in Ontonagon gusted over 50 mph at times during the blizzard event. Wind chills also lowered to 30 below to 40 below zero on the 10th. Area roads and highways were closed due the blizzard conditions as snow amounts totaled four to six inches.

Lake effect snow and blowing snow reduced visibility less than one quarter mile over much of the county.  Extreme blowing and drifting of snow from 40 to 50 mph wind gusts forced the closure of Highway 28 from far eastern Marquette County to Munising on the morning of the 10th as wind chills dropped to 20 below to 30 below zero.  Munising Area Schools were closed on the 11th as roads were still being cleared. Four to six inches of snow were observed during the blizzard event.

Winds gusting over 40 mph at times caused widespread whiteout conditions in lake effect snow and blowing snow, especially along the Lake Superior shoreline. Visibility reported by the Luce County Airport AWOS was one-quarter mile or less through much of the period as wind chills lowered to 20 below zero on the 10th. ||The observer in Two Heart reported a snowfall total of 12 to 14 inches in the 24-hour period ending on the morning of the 10th. Many area roads and highways were closed due to the blizzard conditions.

A 36-male from Wisconsin who was visiting relatives in Escanaba went missing late on the 16th.  Law enforcement found his body in the woods near the northern fence line of the Delta County Airport late on the 18th.  The cause of death was determined to be hypothermia as temperatures were near or below freezing throughout much of the time period.
There was a public mPING report of half dollar sized hail just east of Birch Creek.
The spotter in Rockland measured five inches of lake enhanced snow in approximately nine hours.

An estimated eight inches of wet snow fell in 12 hours near the Houghton-Keweenaw County line based on a similar report from the observer in Kearsarge.  North to northwest winds gusting as high as 45 mph also caused considerable blowing of snow and reduced visibility to one-quarter mile or less at times.
Observers from Merriweather through Bergland Dam to Paulding measured between nine and ten inches of wet snow in approximately 18 hours.

The observer in Twin Lakes measured nearly 16 inches of wet snow in just over 24 hours while observers in Kearsarge and Painesdale measured eight inches of snow in approximately 15 hours. North to northwest winds gusting as high as 45 mph also caused considerable blowing of snow and reduced visibility to one-quarter mile or less at times.

Observers in Herman and Three Lakes measured nearly a foot of wet storm total snowfall while Skanee measured nearly 10 inches.  Northwest winds gusting as high as 35 to 40 mph also caused considerable blowing of snow and reduced visibility to one-quarter mile or less at times.

Storm total snowfall amounts across the county included 20 inches near Little Lake, 18.8 inches at the Marquette National Weather Service Office, approximately 18 inches at both Harvey and Skandia, 17 inches at K.I. Sawyer and between 13 and 14 inches in the city of Marquette.  The wet, heavy snow combined with north to northwest winds gusting as high as 40 to 45 mph at times uprooted several trees in the Marquette-Harvey area and downed power lines as well causing multiple power outages across the county.  There were multiple reports throughout the morning of the 13th of vehicles, including semis, getting stuck in the wet heavy snow.  A plow was called to assist an EMS vehicle stuck near Marquette Mountain.

Significant storm total snowfall amounts over the county included nearly 20 inches at Eben Junction, 16 inches at Munising and 15 inches at Chatham.  The wet, heavy snowfall combined with strong northwest winds gusting as high as 50 mph also caused extensive tree damage and downed multiple trees in Munising across Highway M-94.  Hundreds of power outages were reported across the county.
Storm total snowfall amounts included 11.1 inches in Ironwood and 10.7 inches near Watersmeet.

Storm total snowfall amounts included 13 inches twelve miles northeast of Amasa, 11 inches at Peavy Falls Dam and 10 inches in Amasa.  The wet snow combined with gusty northwest winds of 35 to 40 mph caused sporadic power outages across the county.

Based on adjacent reports, there was estimated eight inches of wet, heavy snow which fell across southern Houghton County during the event.
Storm total snowfall reports ranged from 3 to 6 inches in the Gladstone-Escanaba area to nearly 17 inches in Rock.

The Marquette County Sheriff's Department rescued six swimmers in distress and two from a nearby rock at Little Presque Isle in Marquette on the afternoon of the 11th. First responders then located a number of others stranded out on the island.  Overall, forty people were safely transported back to shore from the island with no injures reported.  Northwest to north winds to 15 mph with gusts to 18 mph were observed that afternoon from nearly marine observation sites.  Strong currents and waves to three feet were reported during the incident.

Three swimmers were rescued from strong currents at Little Presque Isle near Marquette on the afternoon of the 19th.  The swimmers were a 38-year-old male, an 11-year-old male, and a 10-year-old girl.  They were approximately 75 yards away from the shoreline when they were caught in a dangerous current.  A nearby couple rescued all three swimmers and got them back to shore just as the Michigan State Police and U.S. Coast Guard arrived on the scene.  The two children were medically cleared at the scene.  The 38-year-old male was transported to a local hospital for further medical evaluation.  Winds were west at 15 to 20 mph based on nearby observations along the shoreline, and conditions were reported to be choppy.

An unusual low-topped supercell with no lightning produced a brief spin-up of an EF-1 tornado west of Escanaba.  The rotating wall cloud and lowering funnel were observed by travelers on Highway US-2 as the tornado initially touched down near Pete's Pick and Pull Auto Parts snapping and knocking down several trees and utility poles.  A couple of trees fell on one residence in this vicinity.  The tornado then crossed US-2 moving northeastward as it caused extensive damage to to several storage units at Pine Ridge Storage.  The tornado continued northeastward into a wooded area where hundreds of trees were snapped and uprooted.  As the thunderstorm collapsed the damage evolved into downburst wind damage at the end of its path.  The tornado only lasted two minutes.
